'''Mujaddid Ahmed Ijaz''' ([[Urdu]]: {{nq|مجدد احمد اعجا ز}}; June 12, 1937 – July 9, 1992) was a Pakistani-American [[experimental physicist]] noted for his role in discovering new [[isotope]]s<ref name="Roanoke Times">{{cite news |title=Tech Physicist Helps in Finding New Isotopes |author=Robert B. Sears |newspaper=[[The Roanoke Times]] |date=1970-10-17}}</ref> that expanded the neutron-deficient side of the [[Periodic table|atomic chart]]. Some of the isotopes he discovered enabled significant advances in medical research, particularly in the treatment of cancer, and further advanced the experimental understanding of nuclear structures.<ref name="RSC 1">{{cite journal |last1=Ni |first1=Wen-Xiu |last2=Man |first2=Wai-Lun |last3=Cheung |first3=Myra Ting-Wai |last4=Sun |first4=Raymond Wai-Yin |last5=Shu |first5=Yuan-Lan |last6=Lam |first6=Yun-Wah |last7=Che |first7=Chi-Ming |last8=Lau |first8=Tai-Chu |title=Osmium(vi) complexes as a new class of potential anti-cancer agents |journal=Chemical Communications |date=2011 |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=2140–2 |doi=10.1039/C0CC04515B |pmid=21203649}}</ref><ref name="RSC 2">{{cite journal |last1=Shnyder |first1=Steve D. |last2=Fu |first2=Ying |last3=Habtemariam |first3=Abraha |last4=van Rijt |first4=Sabine H. |last5=Cooper |first5=Patricia A. |last6=Loadman |first6=Paul M. |last7=Sadler |first7=Peter J. |title=Anti-colorectal cancer activity of an organometallic osmium arene azopyridine complex |journal=MedChemComm |date=2011 |volume=2 |issue=7 |pages=666 |doi=10.1039/C1MD00075F|url=http://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/38704/1/WRAP_Fu_467_MCC_2011_Ying%20Fu_2_666_deposit.pdf }}</ref> Ijaz conducted his research work at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratories]] (ORNL).<ref name="CSM MMI">{{cite news |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2004/0211/p09s02-cogn.html |title=Not all of Pakistan's nuclear scientists were rogues |author=Mansoor Ijaz |newspaper=[[Christian Science Monitor]] |date=2004-02-11 |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> He and his ORNL colleagues published more than 60 papers in physics journals announcing isotope discoveries and other results of their accelerator experiments from 1968 until 1983.<ref name="MAI NYT">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/07/14/obituaries/mujaddid-ahmed-ijaz-nuclear-scientist-55.html |title=Obituary: Mujaddid Ahmed Ijaz, Nuclear Scientist |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=1992-07-14 |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref>

Ijaz participated in the U.S. ''[[Atoms for Peace]]'' initiative during the 1970s.<ref name="CSM MMI"/> The program provided a number of third-world countries, including Pakistan, with civilian nuclear reactor technology to develop energy for peaceful purposes.<ref name="Atoms">{{cite news |url=http://www.armscontrol.org/act/2003_12/Lavoy |title=The Enduring Effects of Atoms for Peace |author=Peter R. Lavoy |publisher=[[Arms Control Association]] |date=December 2003 |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> As a tenured professor of physics at [[Virginia Tech]], he acted as thesis adviser to graduate students from around the world in experimental physics disciplines. Ijaz made extensive trips abroad during his career, including sabbaticals as a visiting professor at Saudi Arabia's [[King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mishkin |first1=E. A. |last2=Ijaz |first2=M. A. |title=Physics in Saudi Arabia |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1982 |volume=35 |issue=12 |pages=15 |doi=10.1063/1.2914875|bibcode=1982PhT....35l..15M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alamy |first1=F. A. S. |last2=Ijaz |first2=M. |title=Saudi research center |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1983 |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=94–95 |doi=10.1063/1.2915628|bibcode=1983PhT....36d..94A }}</ref> in the early 1980s and as a visiting faculty member at the [[Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in Trieste, Italy in 1985. He retired [[Emeritus|Professor Emeritus]] of Physics from Virginia Tech in December 1991 after a 27-year career in teaching and research.<ref name="MAI NYT"/> Ijaz and his wife emigrated to the United States and settled in Virginia, where they had five children. He died in 1992 after a battle with cancer.

==Early life and education==
[[File:Mujaddid Ijaz with his mother, sisters and brother, circa 1957.png|thumb|left|240px|Ijaz with his mother and siblings, 1957]]
Mujaddid Ijaz was born on June 12, 1937, in [[Baddomalhi]], [[British Indian Empire]]. His father was a medical student who died in his mid-20s of brain cancer. His mother, a homemaker, remarried. He was the third of ten children in his family. Ijaz's early education was made at rural village schools near Baddomalhi. He attended [[Township, Lahore#Schools and colleges|Islamia High School]] in Lahore.<ref name="Floyd 1">{{cite news|title=Dr. Ijaz Promoted|author=Staff Report|publisher=Floyd Press|date=1972-07-06}}</ref> His early interest in science and physics was attributed to his step-father's work in the local meteorology department.

After graduating from high school and finishing college entrance exam requirements, Ijaz was admitted to [[Government College University, Lahore|Government College]] in Lahore.<ref name="MAI NYT"/> There, he majored in physics and graduated with a B.Sc. in 1957. He continued advanced studies under the tutelage of Prof. [[Rafi Muhammad Chaudhry]], widely considered a pioneer in Pakistani [[experimental physics]], until 1959 when he met Razia Begum Nazir. They later married and emigrated to the United States in 1960.<ref name="Floyd 2">{{cite news|title=Pakistan Couple Made American Citizens|author=Staff Report|publisher=Floyd Press|date= 1970-02-12}}</ref>

[[File:Mujaddid & Lubna Ijaz present Quran to Gordon Blackwell, president of Florida State University, 1960.png|thumb|left|240px|Ijaz gives a Quran to Gordon Blackwell, president of [[Florida State University|Florida State]], 1960]]

Ijaz and his wife arrived in [[Tallahassee]], [[Florida]], in August 1960, where they settled as incoming graduate students at [[Florida State University]].<ref name="Floyd 2"/> He developed an early interest in particle physics and accelerator experiments while at [[Florida State University|Florida State]], from where he graduated in June 1962 with a master's degree in physics.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.fsu.edu/alumni/default.asp?aclass=1962|title=Florida State Alumni, Class of 1962|publisher=[[Florida State University]]|author=Alumni Listing|access-date=2014-05-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100609232937/http://www.physics.fsu.edu/alumni/default.asp?aclass=1962|archive-date=2010-06-09|url-status=dead}}</ref> His thesis was titled ''Study of Angular Distributions of Elastically Scattered 8 to 19 Mev Alpha Particles from Al27''<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uO1wPwAACAAJ&q=mujaddid+ijaz|title=Study of Angular Distributions of Elastically Scattered 8 to 19 Mev Alpha Particles from Al27|author=Mujaddid A. Ijaz|publisher=[[Florida State University]]|work=Master's Thesis|year=1962|access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> and from Ohio University in May 1964 with a Ph.D. in Nuclear Physics<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phy.ohiou.edu/people/where.html|title=Ohio Physics & Astronomy Ph.D. Alumni|publisher=[[Ohio University]]|author=Alumni Listing|access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> with a thesis titled ''Proton-Proton Collisions at 2.0 BeV''.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xbX-NwAACAAJ&q=mujaddid+ijaz|title=Proton-Proton Collisions at 2.0 BeV|author=Mujaddid A. Ijaz|publisher=[[Ohio University]]|work=Ph.D. Thesis|year=1964|access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref>

==Academic and scientific research career==
===Virginia Polytechnic Institute===
Mujaddid Ijaz joined the faculty of the [[Virginia Tech]] Physics department in September 1964 as an assistant professor of physics.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JIpYAAAAMAAJ&q=mujaddid+ijaz |title=Directory of Physics Faculties: United States, Canada, Mexico |author=American Association of Physics Teachers |author2=American Institute of Physics |year=1965 |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> In his early years as a faculty member, Ijaz devoted much of his time to his teaching responsibilities,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ijaz |first1=M. A. |title=Motivating students |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1975 |volume=28 |issue=12 |pages=60 |doi=10.1063/1.3069253|bibcode=1975PhT....28l..60I }}</ref> including acting as adviser to the university's roster of graduate students and doctoral candidates. He conducted his early research at the Physics department's newly installed nuclear reactor, which at the time was equipped with a [[neutron activation analysis]] laboratory.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.phys.vt.edu/about/history.shtml |title=Virginia Tech Department of Physics - History |publisher=[[Virginia Tech]], Department of Physics |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> Ijaz's early experimental results earned him an appointment as research collaborator at the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratories]] in 1966 under a ''University Isotope Separator at Oak Ridge'' (UNISOR) grant funded by the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Energy Department]].<ref name="Roanoke Times"/>

In 1974, Ijaz launched a ''Distinguished Visitors Colloquium Series'' under the Physics department's sponsorship that brought world-renowned physicists to the [[Blacksburg, Virginia|Blacksburg]] campus for nearly a decade. Visiting scholars included Salam, [[Sheldon Glashow]], and Nobel physics laureates [[Hans Bethe]], [[Robert Hofstadter]], [[Eugene Paul Wigner|Eugene Wigner]] and [[Richard Feynman]]. Noted Chinese physicist Luke W. Mo (whose group at the [[Stanford Linear Accelerator]] had won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1990) also lectured at Virginia Tech.<ref name="Quarta">{{cite web|url=http://www.phys.vt.edu/newsletters/QuantaSpring2003.pdf|title=2002-2003 Department Retirements - Professor Luke W. Mo|author=Virginia Tech Physics Department|website=Quanta |volume=4 |issue=1 |date=April 2003|access-date=2014-05-02}}</ref>

Ijaz attained the rank of Full Professor of Physics in 1977,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pGgOAQAAMAAJ&q=mujaddid+ijaz |title=National Faculty Directory, Volumes 1-2 |publisher=Gale Research Company |isbn=9780787633738 |year=1992 |access-date=2014-05-01}}</ref> and during the same year served as acting head of the physics department. After several foreign sabbaticals in the 1980s, the first at U.P.M. in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia from 1979 until 1981<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ijaz |first1=M. A. |last2=Khan |first2=M. N. |title=Physics teaching at the University of Petroleum and Minerals |journal=[[Physics Education]] |date=1981 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=223–227 |doi=10.1088/0031-9120/16/4/312|bibcode=1981PhyEd..16..223I |s2cid=250815862 }}</ref> and another at I.C.T.P. in 1985, he continued his teaching duties<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ijaz |first1=M. A. |title=Recognition for teaching |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1977 |volume=30 |issue=8 |pages=11–13 |doi=10.1063/1.3037658|bibcode=1977PhT....30h..11I }}</ref> at Virginia Tech until retirement in December 1991 as Professor Emeritus of Physics. During the latter part of his career, Ijaz published papers that focused on methods and results in teaching,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ijaz |first1=L. R. |last2=Dening |first2=D. C. |last3=Ijaz |first3=M. A. |last4=Jenkins |first4=D. A. |last5=Leinhardt |first5=T. E. |title=Students help to improve laboratory instruction |journal=[[The Physics Teacher]] |date=1978 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=160 |doi=10.1119/1.2339858|bibcode=1978PhTea..16..160I }}</ref> religion and science<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shaw |first1=M. P. |last2=Ijaz |first2=M. A. |title=Restrictions on religion |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1983 |volume=36 |issue=5 |pages=15 |doi=10.1063/1.2915651|bibcode=1983PhT....36e..15S |s2cid=178426203 }}</ref> and other aspects of physics that did not form part of his technical research in earlier years.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Izaz |first1=M. A. |last2=Ijaz |first2=M. M. |title=God as the Ultimate Unifying Force |journal=[[Physics Today]] |date=1988 |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=129 |doi=10.1063/1.2811307 |bibcode=1988PhT....41a.129I}}</ref> Also a physicist and teaching researcher at Virginia Tech, Lubna Razia Ijaz established a scholarship in 1996 that is awarded to students involved in physics education.<ref name="PhysScholarship">{{cite web |url=http://www.phys.vt.edu/awards/Ijaz.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100615050021/http://www.phys.vt.edu/awards/Ijaz.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-date=15 June 2010 |title=Lubna Razia Ijaz Scholarship |publisher=Virginia Tech Department of Physics |access-date=13 April 2015 }}</ref>

===Oak Ridge National Laboratories===
[[File:Mujaddid Ijaz, Dr. Munir Khan & Dr. Abdus Salam, 1972.jpg|thumb|right|240px|Ijaz (left) with [[Munir Ahmad Khan|Munir Khan]] & [[Abdus Salam]] (right), Nathiagali Physics Conference, 1976]]
Mujaddid Ijaz began his research work at the Oak Ridge National Laboratories (ORNL) in 1966 under Virginia Tech funding contributed to the UNISOR program.<ref name="Roanoke Times"/> UNISOR was a consortium at that time of 13 institutions whose research scientists were collaborating at Oak Ridge supported by U.S. Energy Department grants together with [[Oak Ridge Associated Universities]], of which Virginia Tech was one. Ijaz's research focused on the discovery of new [[isotope]]s using ORNL's [[High Flux Isotope Reactor]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.ameslab.gov/files/ric_news/RIC.News.V5/RIC.News.V5.N2.pdf |title=Rare Earth Information Center News |publisher=Institute for Atomic Research, [[Iowa State University]] |date=1970-06-01 |access-date=2014-05-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130316034519/http://www.ameslab.gov/files/ric_news/RIC.News.V5/RIC.News.V5.N2.pdf |archive-date=16 March 2013 }}</ref> The reactor was built in 1965 with the highest [[neutron flux]] of any reactor at the time. It produced more medical isotopes while allowing higher fidelity of materials research than any other reactor available in the U.S. Energy Department's science and energy laboratory system during the 1970s. Ijaz and his colleagues at Oak Ridge, led by Kenneth S. Toth, used the High Flux Reactor to discover new isotopes and map characteristics of existing isotopes, including [[isotope]]s of [[Isotopes of erbium|Erbium]], [[Isotopes of ytterbium|Ytterbium]],<ref name="Erbium+Ytterbium">{{cite journal|url=http://65.54.113.239/Publication/52885530/production-of-rare-earth-alpha-emitters-with-energetic-3he-particles-new-isotopes-151er-156yb|title=Production of Rare-Earth α Emitters with Energetic <sup>3</sup>He Particles; New Isotopes: <sup>151</sup>Er, <sup>156</sup>Yb, and <sup>157</sup>Yb|journal=Physical Review C|volume=2|issue=4|pages=1480|author1=K. During the 1970s, Ijaz participated<ref name="CSM MMI"/> in the ''Atoms for Peace'' initiative created by [[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] in 1953 to help the post-World War II international community cope with nuclear power.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9HUEO7ms6moC|title=Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace|author=Ira Chernus|publisher=[[Texas A&M University Press]]|isbn=9781585442201|year=2002|access-date=2014-05-02}}</ref> Pakistan's first facility, a 5 MW [[Pakistan Atomic Research Reactor#PARR-I Reactor|PARR-I]] pool-type facility, was provided by the United States in 1965.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nuclearfiles.org/menu/key-issues/nuclear-weapons/issues/facilities/pakistani-nuclear-weapons-facilities.htm|title=Pakistan's Nuclear Facilities|publisher=[[Nuclear Age Peace Foundation]]|author=NuclearFiles.org|access-date=2014-05-02}}</ref> The reactor began operations on December 21, 1965, under the supervision of Pakistani scientists led by Abdus Salam.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nti.org/facilities/109/|title=PARR-1 Facility|website=Nuclear Threat Initiative|access-date=2014-05-03}}</ref>

===Notable collaborations===
Mujaddid Ijaz collaborated with notable physicists and mathematicians throughout his 27-year career. Most notable among these were his collaborations with [[Abdus Salam]]<ref name="Newsweek">{{cite magazine|url=http://newsweekpakistan.com/who-is-memogates-mansoor-ijaz/|title=Who in the World is Mansoor Ijaz?|author=Fasih Ahmed| magazine=[[Newsweek Pakistan]]|date=2011-12-02|access-date=2012-05-12}}</ref> whose groundbreaking work in [[electroweak interaction]]s together with American physicists [[Steven Weinberg]] and [[Sheldon Glashow]] earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1979.

In 1976, Salam recommended creating an international forum for the advancement of science and technology to be hosted by Pakistan in the [[Hazara region|Hazara]] region while serving as [[Ministry of Science and Technology (Pakistan)|Science Advisor]] to the [[Prime Minister of Pakistan]]. Since then, the [[International Nathiagali Summer College on Physics|Nathiagali Physics Conferences]] has gathered notable scientists from around the world during summer breaks to break the intellectual isolation faced by Pakistani scientists.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ncp.edu.pk/insc/|title=International Nathiagali Summer College|publisher=National Centre for Physics and [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]]}}</ref> Ijaz participated in these conferences several times during the mid-1970s under [[National Science Foundation]] grants.{{citation needed|date=June 2023}} He was also a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="Roanoke Times"/>

==Personal life==
[[File:Mujaddid Ijaz at his Virginia home with his wife and children ca 1982.png|thumb|right|240px|Mujaddid & Lubna Ijaz with their children in Virginia, 1982]]

Mujaddid Ijaz was an [[Ahmadiyya|Ahmadi]].<ref>{{cite web|first1=Ehsan |last1=Ahmad |access-date=2020-06-29|title=Mansoor Ijaz – The memogate controversy|url=https://www.rabwah.net/mansoor-ijaz-the-memogate-controversy/|date=9 December 2011|website=[[Rabwah Times]]}}</ref> He married Razia Begum (''nee'' Nazir) in June 1960 prior to emigrating to the United States. Razia later took her husband's chosen name, Lubna, when they both became naturalized American citizens on January 5, 1970.<ref name="Messenger">{{cite news|title=Mr. & Mrs. Ijaz Became American Citizens Jan. 5, 1970|author=Staff Reporting|publisher=Montgomery News Messenger|date=1970-01-27}}</ref> They had five children: [[Mansoor Ijaz|Mansoor]], Farouk, Atif and Mujeeb. Neelam, their only daughter, was born in Pakistan.<ref name="Floyd 1"/>

The Ijazes initially settled in Blacksburg, where Virginia Tech was situated, and lived there from 1964 until 1969.<ref name="Messenger"/> After several years of living in the rural community of [[Floyd, Virginia]],<ref name="Floyd 1"/><ref name="Floyd 2"/> they returned to [[Christiansburg, Virginia|Christiansburg]], a township near Virginia Tech, in 1973, building a home in the Appalachian Mountains that today remains the family's homestead.<ref name="Newsweek"/>

Mujaddid Ijaz died on July 9, 1992, at his home in [[Shawsville, Virginia]], of complications arising from a protracted battle with brain and lung cancer.<ref name="MAI NYT"/> He was buried in traditional Muslim rituals at the site of his most favored farm in Alum Ridge, surrounded by a large gathering of his family from around the United States and his physics colleagues and friends from southwestern Virginia. President [[George H. W. Bush]] consoled Ijaz's widow in a [[:File:President George H. W. Bush condolences on Mujaddid Ijaz's death, 1992.png|letter dated July 24, 1992]].
